_why: Kesseboehmer's STEP files carry no materials at all. A glTF primitive with
no material gets the format's DEFAULT material, which is white, fully
METALLIC and fully rough - so every part rendered as white chrome. In the
app that reads as flat and pale; in AR, where the viewer lights the scene
with its own bright environment, it blows out completely. Matt: 'when i
load it in AR is very bright and over exposed.' That is the cause, and it
is one line of the glTF spec rather than anything about the lighting.
Colours here are sRGB, the way a person reads them off a colour picker.
tools/add-materials.mjs converts them to the linear values glTF actually
stores - 27/255 is 0.1059 as a fraction and 0.01096 once linearised, so
writing the sRGB number straight into baseColorFactor would come out
NO NORMAL OR BUMP MAPS, and not by choice: the converted meshes carry
POSITION and nothing else - no UVs - so there is nowhere to put a texture.
Generating UVs for 45 CAD parts is its own job. Roughness does the work
instead, which is most of what a brushed-metal read is anyway.

metal.label: Kesseboehmer steel, dark grey
metal.note: Matt's figure. Metallic below 1.0 because a fully metallic surface with no environment to reflect goes black in some viewers.

plastic.label: YouboXx, lighter grey
plastic.note: Matt's figure. Dielectric, so metallic is zero - plastic that reports itself as metal is the other way to blow out in AR.

timber.label: PWS timber shelf
timber.note: The colour make-timber.py already writes. Kept, so the boards do not change appearance.
